claims.text: What the strip looks like “Sawtooth” flutter waves at an atrial rate of about 300, commonly conducting 2:1 (ventricular rate about 150); regular unless the block varies.
claims.quote: "Sawtooth" ﬂutter waves, typically at ~300 bpm atrial rate Commonly conducts 2:1 (ventricular rate ~150 bpm) Regular unless variable block present

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Atrial rate: about 300 (range 200–400)
claims.quote: resulting in a fairly predictable atrial rate of around 300 bpm (range 200-400)

claims.text: Ventricular rate: a fraction of the atrial rate — 2:1 block = 150, 3:1 = 100, 4:1 = 75
claims.quote: 2:1 block = 150 bpm 3:1 block = 100 bpm 4:1 block = 75 bpm

claims.text: Rhythm: regular unless the block varies
claims.quote: Regular unless variable block present

claims.text: Variable block: the ventricular response is irregular and may mimic AF
claims.quote: The ventricular response is irregular and may mimic atrial fibrillation (AF)

claims.text: Telling it from AF: with variable block, the R-R intervals are multiples of the P-P interval
claims.quote: In atrial flutter with variable block the R-R intervals will be multiples of the P-P interval

claims.text: Flutter waves: inverted “saw-tooth” flutter waves in II, III, aVF; upright flutter waves in V1 that may look like P waves
claims.quote: “Saw-tooth” pattern of inverted flutter waves in leads II, III, aVF Upright flutter waves in V1 that may resemble P waves

claims.text: Baseline: no isoelectric baseline
claims.quote: Loss of the isoelectric baseline

claims.text: QRS: narrow complex tachycardia
claims.quote: Narrow complex tachycardia

claims.text: Clue: a narrow complex tachycardia at 150 (range 130–170) → suspect flutter; turn the ECG upside down and look at II, III and aVF for flutter waves
claims.quote: Narrow complex tachycardia at 150 bpm (range 130-170)? Yes -> Suspect flutter! Turn the ECG upside down and closely examine the inferior leads (II, III + aVF) for flutter waves

claims.text: Vagal maneuvers/adenosine: usually do not convert flutter (unlike AVNRT), but briefly increase the block and can unmask flutter waves
claims.quote: Atrial flutter will not usually cardiovert with these techniques (unlike AVNRT), although typically there will be a transient period of increased AV block during which flutter waves may be unmasked

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism: a re-entry circuit within the right atrium
claims.quote: Atrial flutter is a form of supraventricular tachycardia caused by a re-entry circuit within the right atrium.

claims.text: Typical flutter: the circuit runs through the cavotricuspid isthmus (between the IVC and the tricuspid annulus); the atria fire at 250–350 (typically 300) and the AV node usually lets half through (2:1 block)
claims.quote: Typical atrial flutter is due to a large reentrant circuit involving most of the right atrium and requires conduction between the orifice of the inferior vena cava and the annulus of the tricuspid valve (the cavotricuspid isthmus). The atria depolarize at a rate of 250 to 350 beats/minute (typically 300 beats/minute). Because the atrioventricular (AV) node cannot usually conduct at this rate, typically half of the impulses get through (2:1 block)

claims.text: Causes and hemodynamic effects are similar to AF; many patients with flutter also have periods of AF
claims.quote: Atrial flutter is much less common than atrial fibrillation, but its causes and hemodynamic consequences are similar. Many patients with atrial flutter also have periods of atrial fibrillation.

claims.text: Higher-degree block (3:1, 4:1) is usually due to medications or underlying heart disease
claims.quote: Higher-degree blocks can occur — usually due to medications or underlying heart disease — resulting in lower rates of ventricular conduction, e.g. 3:1 or 4:1 block.

claims.text: 1:1 conduction (sympathetic stimulation, an accessory pathway, or AV-nodal blockers given in WPW) causes severe hemodynamic instability and can progress to VF
claims.quote: Atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction can occur due to sympathetic stimulation, or in the presence of an accessory pathway. The administration of AV-nodal blocking agents to a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome can precipitate this Atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction is associated with severe haemodynamic instability and progression to ventricular fibrillation

claims.text: Symptoms Depend mainly on the ventricular rate and any heart disease: regular and < 120 → few or none; faster rates or variable conduction → palpitations; low cardiac output → chest discomfort, dyspnea, weakness, syncope
claims.quote: Symptoms of atrial flutter depend primarily on ventricular rate and the nature of any underlying heart disorder. If ventricular rate is < 120 beats/minute and regular, there are likely to be few or no symptoms. Faster rates and variable AV conduction usually cause palpitations. Decreased cardiac output may cause symptoms of hemodynamic compromise (eg, chest discomfort, dyspnea, weakness, syncope).

claims.text: Atrial thrombi may form and embolize
claims.quote: Atrial thrombi may form and embolize.

claims.text: Treatment Initial episode: for most patients, electrical conversion (synchronized cardioversion or overdrive pacing) is the treatment of choice — mandatory with 1:1 conduction or hemodynamic compromise; low energy (50 J) usually works
claims.quote: Thus, for most patients, electrical conversion (using synchronized cardioversion or overdrive pacing) is the treatment of choice for an initial episode and is mandatory with 1:1 AV conduction or hemodynamic compromise. Typically, low-energy (50 joules) conversion is effective.

claims.text: Rate control with drugs is harder than in AF
claims.quote: Pharmacologic rate control is more difficult to achieve in atrial flutter than in atrial fibrillation.

claims.text: Drug conversion: control the rate first with beta blockers or nondihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) — class Ia and Ic drugs can otherwise allow 1:1 conduction
claims.quote: If medication is used to restore sinus rhythm, rate must first be controlled with beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil, diltiazem). Many of the antiarrhythmic medications that can restore sinus rhythm (especially class Ia and Ic) can slow atrial flutter, shorten AV nodal refractoriness (by their vagolytic effects), or do both enough to allow 1:1 conduction

claims.text: Anticoagulation: usually needed before cardioversion; long-term for chronic or recurrent flutter
claims.quote: Anticoagulation is usually necessary before cardioversion. Long-term oral anticoagulation to prevent stroke is required for patients with chronic or recurrent atrial flutter.

claims.text: Cure: an ablation line across the cavotricuspid isthmus cures typical flutter in > 95%
claims.quote: placement of an ablation line of block across the isthmus will cure typical atrial flutter in > 95% of patients
